data.title: Menadione (vitamin K3) injection
data.summary: IX Miscellaneous · Synthetic water-soluble vitamin K analogue (provitamin; menadione sodium bisulfite)
data.body:
_Injectables · IX Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Synthetic water-soluble vitamin K analogue (provitamin; menadione sodium bisulfite)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted in the liver to active vitamin K2 (menaquinone-4)
- Vitamin K is a cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S)
- Corrects bleeding from vitamin K deficiency, but acts slowly and weakly compared with vitamin K1

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble — does not need bile for absorption (useful in obstructive jaundice)
- Onset slower than phytomenadione (vitamin K1); not reliable for reversing warfarin

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Hypoprothrombinaemia due to vitamin K deficiency: obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics, prolonged parenteral nutrition
- Used as a haemostatic in some Indian practice
- Not the drug of choice for warfarin reversal or haemorrhagic disease of the newborn — phytomenadione (vitamin K1) is preferred

## Dose & formulations
- Typically 10 mg IM/IV (menadione sodium bisulfite) as directed by the product
- Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) for comparison: newborn prophylaxis 1 mg IM at birth; warfarin reversal 1–10 mg slow IV (no faster than 1 mg/min)

## Adverse effects
- Haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency
- Neonates: haemolysis, hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus — contraindicated
- Vitamin K injection-site skin reactions (mostly with vitamin K1): itchy eczematous plaques at the injection site (early), and later sclerodermoid plaques with a 'cowboy belt' distribution on the buttocks and thighs (Texier disease)
- Rapid IV vitamin K1: anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, collapse)

## Contraindications
- Neonates and infants; late pregnancy (risk to the newborn)
- G6PD deficiency
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antagonises warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists
- Long-term antibiotics (cephalosporins) and cholestyramine increase vitamin K needs

## Monitoring
- Prothrombin time/INR

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid menadione in late pregnancy (neonatal haemolysis and jaundice); vitamin K1 is safe.

## Viva points
- Menadione (K3) vs phytomenadione (K1): K1 is preferred in neonates and for warfarin reversal
- Menadione causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and kernicterus in newborns
- Skin reactions to vitamin K injections: eczematous plaques; Texier disease (pseudo-scleroderma, cowboy-belt pattern)

## Note on sources
Menadione is not covered in Wolverton. Khopkar and standard pharmacology texts were used; please check whether your examiners mean menadione (K3) or phytomenadione (K1).

_Sources: Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements); pharmacology references; Wolverton 4e (drug eruption sections). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
